Question: Did the Apollo lunar landers have airlocks or did they simply release air before opening their hatch?

The LM had an overhead crew transfer hatch for movement between it and the docked Command Module, and it had a forward hatch that was larger and squared off for exiting down the ladder while wearing a PLSS backpack. In practice though, they simply opened the valve to vent the cabin, then pried really hard on the hatch till the seal broke and let out that little remaining pressure, blasting dust out across the lunar surface.

In general, a pathogenic disease is a race between the pathogen your your immune response. When the pathogen is reproducing faster than it’s being destroyed, you grow sicker. When the opposite is true, you grow well. If the opposite is never true, you eventually die. But there’s more to it even than this. While you are fighting off the pathogen, it’s not just killing cells but scrambling their behavior, and your immune response causes inflammation, reallocation of resources, and the release of all sorts of hormones that affect the progression of the disease. In many cases, the pathogen relies on side effects of the immune response such as coughing, sneezing, vomiting or other excretions to spread itself to other hosts. In the case of SARS-Cov-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, not only does it do that, but it causes infected cells to release chemicals that inhibit your immune response and may even cause the immune system to more quickly forget previous exposure, making herd immunity harder to achieve and vaccination less effective. And more directly to the point, when cells are killed are disrupted in large numbers, this results in systemic injuries that cause the body to mount a rough and ready response that can actually cause more damage in the long run in order to survive now. COVID-19, in particular, can cause a run-away immune cascade with can fill the lungs with deadly fluid in a desperate attempt to get the upper hand over the virus, which in the meantime causes the circulatory system to become leaky, both expanding the tissues and therefore possible routes to other hosts that the virus is infecting, and also causing widespread clotting of a sort appropriate to acute injury, but in COVID, leading to distributed scarring and damage to organs throughout the body. So yes, disease is a race, but COVID's a race that can maim even the winner if it gets its hooks in deep enough, so better to stay well out of its clutches. Question: What does it mean when delegates to a convention say ‘*x* votes present & *y* ballots cast’ in the roll call?
Answer: It means exactly that. The roll call is also the first round vote, so you announce the number of delegates present and how they all vote. For a number of reasons, this is largely ceremonial in recent decades, but in fact it’s a real vote in which delegates elected by the state primaries & caucuses cast votes to decide which candidates the party will nominate for election. If no candidate achieves a majority in the first round, additional rounds of voting follow until the party hammers out a selection. This situation has become increasingly rare, but it is possible. The roll call is necessary because in a contested vote, delegates must be present to vote. In modern times, however, voting is usually “ceremonial” because many states have laws requiring delegates to vote initially for the ticket selected during the state party primary or caucus. In most cases, if the primaries produce a clear majority, the convention vote is ceremonial because delegates’ hands are tied by state law. But if the primaries are sufficiently close and the initial vote doesn’t reach a majority, delegates are released to vote as they choose on subsequent rounds. The last contested party convention was the 1976 RNC, during which incumbent President Gerald Ford narrowly won nomination on the first round. In 2024, state party primaries & caucuses selected the Biden / Harris ticket by a clear majority, but Biden then withdrew, leaving Harris to choose a new running mate. This was completely straightforward and non-controversial and is the same thing that would have happened had the head of the ticket died or become incapacitated. Anyone saying otherwise is either ignorant or lying in an attempt to push your emotional buttons by making a rather obvious procedural necessity sound like an assault on democracy. Question: If it is true that natural selection does not favor the lower viability of hybrids, why do hybrids so often have lower viability? Specifically address the issue with an example of a species created through polyploidy.
Answer: Not exactly. Every animal on the planet is, in a sense, a hybrid—of the parents that gave rise to it. But that’s not what you are talking about. You are talking about hybrids like mules that are produced by cross-breeding between species, not within species as in every other living thing. But here, in just restating the question, we’re already a bit in hot water, because “species” is an artificial, construct that isn’t that well grounded in reality. “Species” is a categorization useful for human educational and practical purposes, but it doesn’t reflect the way nature really works, and that mismatch is what gives rise to questions like this. We teach elementary school students that a species is a group of living things that can interbreed with each other, an we display species on the branches of a simple-to-understand tree to show their relatedness. We teach that in the rare cases that different branches interbreed at all, they are unlikely to do so productively, and even less likely to produce fertile young. And that’s true enough if you use that definition of “species” and try to apply it to reality. But when you do that, you have a very wrong understanding of how live changes over time, and so you run into problems. “The tree of life” is a useful way to teach children about the living things around them today, but life isn’t a tree; it’s a fuzzy progression of co-evolving populations that dissolve into and out of one another over time. To ignore that is to overlook the very core of the evolutionary process that gives rise to the variety of life: So let’s put that elementary school definition of “species” aside and look at how life really changes over time—in the real, actual world. So now we have the foundation needed to answer your question: “why do hybrids so often have lower viability.” The simple answer is because we have defined “hybrid” that way, using the oversimplified “tree of life” model, as a crossing between the tips of closely-related branches. In other, we have defined “hybrid” as a cross between individuals in subpopulations that aren’t interfertile. Natually, when you define it that way, reproductive success will be low. But then the fact that any sort of reproduction is possible at all should be a powerful clue you’ve missed something—and you have. Under the “tree of life” model, a better way of thinking on hybrids is as crosses between branches that are just in the process of splitting, that are still so close the touch and are intertwined. Then it makes a little more sense, but even do you soon find the model doesn’t work when you dig into the biological details. Another thing we teach schoolchildren is that different species can’t interbreed because they don’t have the same chromosomes. That’s only sort of mostly true. In fact, chromosomes are just packaging for keeping the DNA safe in the cell. In order to reproduce, the chromosomes are unpacked, and what really counts are the genes—the actual sequence of genetic codes for putting amino acids together to make proteins. Of course, it’s a little more complicated than that. The chromosomes contain start and end markers (telomeres) and sort of attachment points in the middle (centromeres) and in between these, genes for certain things appear in a certain order. For two individuals to breed, the genes from both parents need to appear in the same places, otherwise instead of genetic recombination (variation) you get gibberish, so no crossing people with oak trees, that’s just not going to work. And before the genes can even line up, the cellular machinery has to get them there, in part using the telomeres and centromeres as a guide, so it’s logical to think that if both parents don’t even have the same chromosomes, fertilization is hopeless, and that’s mostly true. Any chromosomal abnormality can revent fertilization from happening at all, or can deprive the fertilized egg of essential genes, leading to genetic disease or outright failure to grow. However, this is not always so. For example, there are humans alive today who have one fewer chromosomes than they rest of us. This is possible due to a mistake during the production of and egg or sperm in which two chromosomes are mistakenly fused, garbling the telomeres meant to mark the end of one and the beginning of the other, but leaving the genes of both intact. Such a fusion makes it harder for fertilization to occur, but it’s not impossible, and the resulting cell when it does work is basically normal. And that’s a good thing because all humans carry a fusion of two chromosomes that are still separate in all the other apes. Sometime, about seven million years ago, this fusion appeared and made it harder for the mutants to interbreed with the other apes around them. It wasn’t impossible, however, and the mutants did okay, eventually creating the Internet. Now, you asked about polyploidy, or individuals having more than one complete set of chromosomes. When this happens through hybridization, the first-generation hybrid (before chromosome doubling) often has reduced fertility because the chromosomes from each parent may not pair correctly during meiosis. This can result in unbalanced gametes, leading to sterility. Indeed, this is very simillar to the reason living humans with a fused pair of chromosomes have fertility problems, and it’s also the reason mules are sterile (though they are not polyploid). Once chromosome doubling does occur, however, the chromosomes from each parent now line up in matching pairs. These line up normally during meiosis, producing balanced gametes, and possibly a new, fully fertile hybrid.

Answer: As in other mammals, lactase production is high during infancy, but after weaning, lactase production typically decreases because, in the absence of milk in the diet, there’s no need for lactase. In humans lacking the MCM6 gene which controls the expression of the LCT gene, LCT expression declines with age, reducing the availability of lactase and the ability to digest lactose.

Question: Why did nature create life? How would it benefit from this creation?
Answer: The anthropomorphism implicit in this question… Let me rephrase that. The way you asked this question makes it clear that you are thinking of nature like a person. That’s understandable, as a big part of the human brain is devoted to understanding and figuring out the intent of other people. But it’s wrong, quite wrong, dangerously wrong. It’s called “animism,” and it’s the way small children and primitive people who no absolutely nothing view the world. But you are not a small child or a primitive person, and you have come here and asked the question, and that’s an absolutely brilliant thing to do—a thing more people should do and more often. The universe (nature) is not a person. It doesn’t do things for a reason (to gain something). Instead, things happen because the forces of nature set things up to be that way. The tide doesn’t come in because it helps the shorebirds. Shorebirds are at the shore when the tide comes in because they have evolved to make a living that way. The tide comes in because wind and the gravity of the moon and the sun and the rotation of the Earth make the tide come in. When the tide comes in, the seawater crashes ashore and makes sea foam. The foam is not there for a reason. The foam is the result of chemical bonds between water molecules and molecules dissolved in the water. Seafoam is made by chemistry, and anywhere in the universe the right conditions are present, similar bubbles and foam will form. Similarly, anywhere in the universe that conditions allow it, amino acids will form (they literally rain down on Earth from space, and we know there exist vast clouds of them in space, made by radiation and simple molecules made inside stars. Anywhere in the universe that conditions allow it, amnio acids will join up to form lipids, and the lipids will form bubbles, and the bubbles will grow and divide very much like living cells, very much like soap bubbles. These little replicating lipid spheres are not alive, but they are chemically very similar to living cell membranes, only simpler. When they form on a planet where no life exists, they will go on endlessly replicating until inevitably, they blunder into chemicals that make them more stable. Then, those more stable little bubbles will continue replicating, outcompeting all the others until they dominate the environment, until the blunder into some molecule that makes them more stable still, and so on. Some of these blunders, we’ve already observed. Some, we can only speculate. But we know enough to see that all the building blocks of life are there, that the entire universe must be filled with them, that it only takes time and opportunity, and life must necessarily appear. It doesn’t appear for any benefit, nor does it die for any benefit when a star explodes and an impact reduces a planetary surface to lava, wiping out all life just as likely happened a few times on the early Earth. It happens because the forces of nature make it happen, no magic, planning, or intelligence required. Now, as to why the forces of nature are what they are, we do not and probably can never know. And not knowing is okay. Far better to perceive and accept the limits of knowledge than pretend to knowledge we can never have, and base our lives upon mistakes and biases.

Question: If evolution is adaptation to the environment, how could the genetic code split and form different creatures but in the same environment? If it *even was* the same environment. Shouldn't we have only one type of creature in an ecosystem?

Even in a single population living in the same environment, variations between individuals cause differences in behavior and tolerance to risk, desire for novelty, and all sorts of things that cause some individuals to interact with that environment differently than others. That can lead to sub-populations using a different strategy for success, and ultimately evolving into an entirely different species. This is exactly what happened with humans. At some point about 7 million years ago, a subpopulation of apes ancestral to us started spending most of their time on the ground. This wasn’t because the tree had vanished, it was because some of the apes developed a different relationship with the trees and the ground that was successful, even while their relatives remained happily content staying mostly up in the branches more like modern chimpanzees. This might have been caused by a thinning of the trees due to climate change, but if so, it was the same forest that the two subpopulations shared, it’s just that they reacted to it differently. This ultimately led our ancestors to move out into more open environments, encounter different threats and challenges, and undergo behavioral and genetic adaptation at an accelerated rate, punctuated by a series of climate swings, migrations, and cullings that made them every more of what they already were, bipedal, pattern matching, tool-making apes.

In so doing, imperfect copies are made just as in all living cells, not all variants fare equally well, and so the viruses evolve, just like the organisms they infect do. Whether you consider that “alive” or not doesn’t change how it works and what it is. The reality is, life isn't a magical state of being poofed into existence by a fairy, it’s just what carbon-based chemistry does given the opportunity, and spans the gamut from simply replicating molecules to advanced, civilization-building whatevers.

Question: Why do viruses want to replicate themselves?
Answer: Why do soap bubbles want to form? Viruses don’t want anything. This anthropomorphic thinking is at the heart of a huge amount of misunderstanding of the natural world, and it’s a big part of why do many people fail to understand how evolution works. Prions don’t want to make animals sick, they are literally nothing more than proteins folded in a way contrary to how life normally folds them, that act as catalytic patterns causing other proteins around them to adopt the same, biologically harmful, replicating structure. Lipid microspheres don’t want to self-replicate any more than soap bubbles want to form, but when exposed to the right conditions in a laboratory, simple osmotic gradients and mechanical forces cause them to grow and divide, and on the early Earth before true life appeared these little marvels—chemically very similar to living cell membranes but much simpler—almost certainly contributed to the appearance of life. RNA doesn’t want to form, but in certain conditions in briny water full of the sorts of amino acids that rain down from space in meteorites, phosphodiester chemical bonds cause nucleotides to form and ice chrystals mechanically stabilize them, and once RNA or RNA-like molecules form, they can act as patterns triggering the formation of copies in a manner not dissimilar to how prions spread. Viruses don’t want to replicate, they are just fragments of RNA or DNA, sometimes encased in protein shells, that on contact with appropriate living host cells coopt those cells to make copies of them. Living populations don’t want to evolve to better fit their environment, every living population is the result of the death or attrition of those members less well-adapted. Biological evolution is not a force driving populations toward perfection, fitness, or complexity, it’s the result (the logically unavoidable result, in fact) of populations producing varied offspring, not all of whom survive or reproduce with equal success. Thus, no intelligence is needed to explain the existence or evolution of life. Life is the logically necessary consequence of chemical elements just doing what they do, anywhere in the universe conditions allow for sufficiently long. The universe may not be filled with little green men or space-fairing blobs, but it is teeming with life, you can count on it.

Question: What is a conventional nuclear weapon, and how does it differ from a nuclear bomb or missile?
Answer: A conventional weapon is one based on conventional, or chemical explosives, typically that release energy from chemical bonds, so “conventional nuclear weapon” is a contradiction in terms. Nuclear weapons come in two forms, fission devices (often called atomic bombs, though not so much anymore) and fusion devices (often called hydrogen bombs, even though they are more likely to be based on lithium deuteride. Fission bombs release energy by breaking heavy, atomically unstable atoms into smaller atoms. Fusion bombs work by releasing (far more) energy by fusing lighter atoms into heavier atoms. If that seems contradictory, you’re not the first person to think so, but it isn’t. For complicated reasons I’m not even going to attempt to go into here, but the element with the least atomic binding energy is iron. So simplifying quite a bit, breaking apart any element heavier than iron, or fusing together any element lighter than iron, releases energy. Fission bombs were called atom bombs because, well, that’s what they are. Fusion bombs were called hydrogen bombs because the easiest element to fuse, and the one used in initial experiments, is hydrogen. In practice, however, hydrogen isn’t practical in a bomb, weapons fuse lithium instead, and to get enough heat and pressure to do it, they need a fission bomb as a trigger, and so are called “thermonuclear” bombs. If this topic interests you, the story I’m working on might too. There is another type of nuclear weapon that is believed to be possible but that will almost certainly never be practical, and another which I certainly hope is not possible but might be…maybe…with careful engineering if the planets align just right. The existence of either would result in bombs as powerful as any military could desire with no radiation beyond a gamma burst at the moment of detonation. Probably impossible, but interesting, so stay tuned.

Question: What happens if every 0 becomes 1 and 1 becomes 0 in every computer in the world?
Answer: Every computer will crash instantly. At its heart, every computer is an intricate set of gates, connected together to perform the Boolean algebraic operations AND, OR, or NOT. Atop this is built a system by which sets of bits (electric signals) are moved, one after the other, into sets of gates arranged into registers where they are operated upon by sets of gates that perform arithmetic and logic operations, such as addition or comparison. These operations follow a sequence of instructions given by a program. At each tick of the system clock, sets of gates are opened or closed so as to move data through the system. Instructions are interpreted by the CPU through a process called the fetch-decode-execute cycle. In, for example, the decode step, a series of bits is broken up into an operation code, and operands. The opcode determines what is done with the operands, where they are moved, how they are manipulated, and what is then done with them. Tick-tick-tick, the clock sets and resets its signal, triggering state changes among the many parts in a predictable, repeating pattern. The actual process—as the very deepest machine code level—is dictated entirely by the ones and zeros of the opcodes and operands, instructions and addresses, the CPU has absolutely no idea what any of it means beyond matching and moving the bits and manipulating the gates. So, what happens if you swap all the 1s and 0s? You create gibberish. Here is a simple program that loads a value in memory using the instruction set of the venerable 8080 CPU: If you swap all the bit, you get this: Yeah…that’s not gonna work. And that’s pretty typical. In every case, the CPU is never going to make it more than a handful of instructions before hitting a loop, impossible state, or simply a number that cannot be interpreted as a command at all.

Question: How did the engineers fit a nuclear reactor into the Mars Curiosity Rover?
Answer: They didn’t, though they could have had they needed so. Curiosity, like the Voyager probes, the Pioneer probes, the Apollo ALSEP packages, and quite a few other space probes (and for that matter, Cold War era Siberian beacons and transmitters) were powered by almost the simplest power source you can imagine, almost as simple (in operation if not actual construction) to a flashlight battery—radioisotope thermoelectric gernerators. There was no “reactor.” I mass of plutoniom-238 glowing red hot with radioactive decay heat is mounted inside an insulated sleeve, surrounded by thermocouples which carry the heat away to a radiator that rejects it into the environment. The movement of heat across the thermocouple causes a flow of electricity. Simple. The device is so simple, the Russians once made one poor peasants could use to power a small radio from the heat of a kerosene lamp. That’s not a joke. Of course, kerosene lamps are sort of wildly inappropriate for spacecraft, so they tend to use plutonium-238, which produces only easily shielded radiation and has a half life that can give the RTG a useful life on the order of a century, or at the very least several decades, which is handy for bobbing about between worlds. Curiosity has just such an RTG, an MMRTG designed to produce over 100 watts continuously for 14 years (the actually output starts higher and declines over time). The MMRTG (the thing shown below with fins) masses 94 pounds (45 kilograms), is about the size of a half-bushel basket, and is mounted on Curiosity’s posterior. Contrary to what you saw in the movie The Martian, an RTG would never be buried. It’s radiation is entirely contained, so it posses no hazard unless torn open, and it cannot work unless the radiators are exposed and able to radiate heat. Buried on Mars, it would stop working once the soil around it warmed up, and then would overheat and rupture—releasing the plutonium cooties. But even though Curiosity didn’t have a reactor, past spacecraft have and future spacecraft will. Most such systems proposed thus far are still thermoelectric generators, they just use a simple fission reactor rather than a static slug of radioactive material to produce the heat, and this makes it possible to generate far more heat and to regulate heat production to maintain stable operation over time. Once such system is the Kilopower generator currently under development by NASA which produces over 4 kilowatts in a 640 pound (290 kg) package, including the radiator and shielding. This fact it, fission reactors are not fundamentally complex. They just require a certain mass of fissionable material and a means of controlling the speed and absorption of neutrons. Industrial power reactors are large an complex because they generate huge amounts of power and must be operated and services safely for decades. Small fission reactors are possible and have long been built for research, demonstration, and testing purposed, and also for medium size generation, including by Soviet and U.S. radar satellites launched in some numbers during the Cold War, and for the most part still up there. Even the so-called “Demon Core” that killed two men and injured dozens was a simple (and crude) fission reactor that use proximity and beryllium neutron reflection blocks for (inadequate) regulation. It was a reactor, it just wasn’t intended every to be allowed to maintain criticality long enough the heat up.

Question: Why is natural evolution referred to as a scientific fact and scientific truth and not a theory?
Answer: Because among educated people, words often have more specific meanings than you might casually suppose. What most people casually call a theory — an idea that might or might be true — an actually calls an hypothesis. Science progresses by posing hypotheses and then investigating to try ans prove them wrong. If they hold up to such scrutiny and seem to fit into an overall model of how things work, then the hypothesis is promoted to observation. Observations are gathered together under models that draw together everything know about a phenomenon, and those models are called “theories.” A theory is not “just an idea that might or might not be true.” A theory is an organized model, consistent with all known evidence, of how a known phenomena works. We have a theory of disease to explain how disease works. We have a theories of gravity because gravity exists. We do not have a theory of unicorn flatulence because unicorns do not exist. We do not have a theory of soothsaying or alien abduction because no latte how many claim the contrary, we have no actual evidence that soothsaying or alien abduction are real things that actually happen. We do have a theory of biological evolution, and it explains how live evolves. The fact that life evolves is an observation, a fact known since antiquity.

Question: Doesn’t new life need inherited genetic material from parents such as DNA and chromosomes? How does abiogenesis life from death work?
Answer: Not to get started, no. The sophisticated heritable genetics used by life today is needed to evolve complex forms, but the only requirement for evolution to happen is that it can replicate and that the replication is not quite perfect. You don’t need genes for that. and as long as that’s true (and nothing gets in the way of it) evolution is a logically unavoidable result. Simple lipid microspheres can spontaneously arise and self replicate in conditions so simple, they can be set up in a high school chemistry lab and would certainly have existed on the early Earth. The chemistry is no more complicated that that behind soap bubbles, and the result is not essentially different from the membrane of a living cell—its just simpler and less stable. And remember, genes are not computer programs. Ultimately DNA is mostly just a shape template for RNA, which is a shape template for proteins. Today, there’s a lot of machinery around it that helps turn those proteins into structure and enzymes into action, but ultimately, all of it boils down to influencing chemistry to do basically what it does anyway. On a planet devoid of life but possessing the right conditions, trillions upon trillions of self-replicating lipid microspheres are eventually doing to stumble upon a contaminant that makes them more stable in some way, and no matter how small that change is, it will quickly dominate. Meanwhile, RNA molecules can also self-assemble and then “self-catalyze” a fancy way of saying they make copies of themselves. Amino acids, lipids, and sugar can form inorganically through a variety of means, and all offer useful components to any evolving proto-life. There are a lot of simpler steps between microspheres and what we consider “true” cells, but it take remarkable recalcitrant to pretend that, given the opportunity, those steps are not a necessary consequence of chemistry and ultimately physics. Life is ubiquitous in the universe. You can take that to the bank. We may never know that exact steps by which it arose on Earth, but that such steps can and must occur anywhere in the universe conditions allow is absolutely clear.

Question: How does gravity hold people, buildings, and huge oceans struck to the Earth’s surface but cannot pull down a balloon?
Answer: Gravity does pull down on a floating balloon. But it also pulls down on all the air around the balloon. This causes the air (the whole atmosphere) to compress so that it’s densest near the ground and thinnest near space. This compression causes the air to pressure on itself and everything in it—including the balloon, and this pressure on the balloon—slightly greater on the lower half than the upper half due to the density gradient of the air, balances the pull of gravity. Question: If there is no possibility that two animals can bear fertile offspring unless they have the same number of chromosomes, how is Universal Common Ancestor a theory and not a hypothesis?
Answer: It’s almost as if your understanding of genetics is wrong. And it is. Don’t feel bad. We do a terrible job in schools of coming back and correcting the oversimplifications taught to young children to get the main idea across. Chromosomes are actually mostly just packaging that protects and supports the genes. The genes so the actual coding (for enzymes, proteins, and “assembly instructions” and as long as they can be read by the cellular machinery, they’ll do their thing. Now of course, some of the worst and most lethal mutations are chromosome level. That’s because they can eliminate or scramble large sections of the genome. That’s bad, but it doesn’t always happen that way. What counts is, can the right genes still be transcribed in the right order when they need to be? And sometimes, the answer is “yes” even with a different number of chromosomes—and you, dear reader, are living proof. Your #2 chromosome is a fusion of two of the chromosomes that all apes have. The evidence for this is clear. Chromosomes contain non-coding structures, centromeres that act as attachment points that help control the chromosome during cell division and telomeres that act as “end of file” markers during transcription. Each chromosome has a centromere in the roughly the middle and a telomere at each end. Except your chromosome #2 has a non-coding segment in the middle where two telomeres were overlayed atop one another and garbled—then two ape chromosomes were fused in an accidental but not particularly uncommon replication mistake several million years ago. Telomere don’t code for anything and these were garbled to the point of uselessness, so the cellular machinery just ignores them—just as it does one of the centromere that is now stranded, marooned uselessly in the now merged chromosome. Other then than these two relics of two different chromosomes having been merged end-to end, all the rest of the DNA is still intact, and all the genes are still in the same places they are in all the other apes, minus a few percent of the mutations that make us human. Logic alone dictates that an animal can interbreed with another with differing chromosome count, since we exist, but we actually have more direct proof: humans are alive today with one few chromosome pairs than the rest of us—humans with an additional chromosomal fusion—and at least one of them went to see a fertility doctor, who analyzed his genome, found the fusion, and with a computer model showed that while the odds of successful fertilization with a normal woman are reduced, he can raise a family if he just keeps trying—but there’s a good change any children will have the same fusion. All of which is completely consistent with what we know to be true. Evolution is not a force driving the adaptation of individuals, rather, it’s the result of a population having many and varies offspring, not all of which survive equally. When a population splits, the two sub-populations inevitably diverge and given time, will eventually lose cross fertility. But long before that happens, they will become more and more different, making interfertility less common, less attractive, and eventually more anatomically and genetically difficult. Having a different number of chromosomes can make it much more difficult, but not necessarily impossible, and where there’s a will (and a noted dearth of Internet porn) there’s a way.

Question: Are humans the ultimate edition of evolution?

Humans are in many ways the dominant life form, but for all our infrastructure and disruption, we would die without microbes—so are we, really? Humans are certainly the most intelligent species ever to appear on Earth, yet many of us use that intelligence to rationalize magical thinking that reduces our brain to a very, very expensive maintainer of blind instinct, while many of us us it to invent ways of killing each other or blindly disrupting our ecosystem on an industrial scale. Question: We are taught that a negative x a negative is a positive. I'm not questioning that. What real life everyday example can you give to prove that, say using apples or cars or people or birds or money or whatever?
Answer: I assume you are referring to algebraic notation, something like a + b = c where b is negative so the equation is the same as a - b = c. Imagine you have a bathtub filled up to a line with water. The taps are off and the drain is securely stopped. Now imagine you have a pain bucket filled with five gallons of water. The water level in the tub is “a.” The bucket is “b.” “c” is the water level in the tub after dumping the bucket into the tub. It shouldn’t surprise you that the water level “c” is higher than the water level “a”. Now start over, with the water level “a” at the line in the tub, the the bucket empty. Now “c” is the waster level in the tub after dunking the bucket in the tub, allowing it to fill, then tossing the bucketful at a passing reindeer. You should, equally, see that the water level “c” must be lower than the level “a.” If you don’t, give it a try. You can (and probably should) substitute a nice pot of begonias for the reindeer.Now, with multiplication, things are a little more complicated. A x B = C might be represented as A being the ingredients for dough and B a baker. Multiply the ingredients by the efforts of one baker, and you get one loaf of bread. Multiple the ingredients by the efforts of ten bakers and get ten loaves. It’s not quite as neat an analogy but you can get the idea if you don’t strain it too hard. Now for negative numbers, replace ingredients with credit card debt and bakers with hunger teenagers. Multiply your bread by ten hunger teenagers and you need to buy more ingredients to replace your empty stores.

Question: Assume humans visited a planet where life evolved but never made the leap past single-cell organisms. Would such organisms ignore us or would they be capable of infecting and killing us?
Answer: We cannot know. On Earth, it took 60 million years after plants evolved lignin, the protein that makes woody plants stiff, for microbes to evolve a way to break it down. During that time—which we call the Carboniferous—wood essentially could not rot. When plants and shrubs died, their soft parts decayed, but the stems and trunks simply feel to the ground and were buried, eventually becoming compressed and modified by geologic processes into seam of coal. So if we encountered a situation like that, we might be safe. Except that lignin is a complex, durable polymer. Life on Earth is vitally dependent on lots of simple lipids and sugars. Alien life, arising on any planet that was remotely Earth-like, would also use lipids and sugars, and very possibly solvents, enzymes, and catalysts that act on them. An alien microbe might be able to infect Earth life while being invisible or immune to our defenses. Or it might be unable to infect us, but might be accidentally poisonous or corrosive to us. Question: Do airplanes bring in fresh air? How do airplane cabins get oxygen?

The first part of any gas turbine engine is the compressor: The compressor is there because the engine needs the same thing you do, oxygen, and it can’t get enough fast enough to operate, especially at high altitudes. The compressor fixes that, and with enough excess capacity to bleed compressed air off into the cabin. This air is at much higher pressure than the cabin, and a pressure regulated valve allows air to escape the cabin, maintaining a stable pressure inside and replacing all the air in the cabin with fresh, warm air every 2–3 minutes, and while there, it circulates through 3–4 row cells, being conditioned and filtered on each circuit, so it’s unquestionably the cleanest air city dwellers will ever breath. That’s in flight, of course. Sitting on the ground with an engine running, you will often swell traces of exhaust that get sucked into the cabin.

Name: C Stuart Hardwick
Question: Were the Apollo’s Ascent Module Engine (part of the LM) tested pre-flight? I can’t see how they could be other than static testing non-flying units. Am I missing something or was NASA taking a big risk with each one that went to the moon?
Answer: Let me ask you this (bear with me): If I swing a hammer at your head, how likely are you to duck? Pretty likely, I’ll wager. I mean, a hammer only needs momentum to hurt when it hits you, and unless I get hit by a train between the time I wind up and the time I make contact, ducking’s a good plan, yes? To be clear, the APS design was rigorously and exhaustively tested on the ground, by remote control in Earth orbit, by crewed missions to Earth orbit and by the Apollo 10 mission to the moon before ever trusting a human life to it. What you may have heard (and misunderstood) was that the individual APS for a given mission was never fueled and test fired before the mission. That’s true, but it’s also true of all the RCS thrusters on all Apollo spacecraft and the Saturn rocket. So here’s the thing. The Apollo APS engine wasn’t as simple as a hammer, but it was about as simple as high-performance rockets get. The propellants, when mixed, could not fail to combust explosively, that was simple chemistry. The propellants were stored inside polymer bags into metal tanks. Injecting helium between the tank wall and the bag would push the propellant out, and the helium pressure could be checked ahead of time and was from multiply redundant high pressure sources, stepped down through trivially simple mechanical pressure regulators—which were tested before assembly. The pressurant gas was admitted into that space by redundant one-way pyrotechnic actuated, electrically fired valves, either of which could do the job alone. The engine was fired by means of an ingenious multiply redundant, electrically triggered pneumatic valve that ensured that when the circuit was closed, both propellants would flow pretty much no matter what any two things went wrong inside the mechanism. And the rest was just physics. It really couldn’t fail unless damaged, and the quickest way to damage it was to fire it up. Doing so would expose all the internal plumbing and moving parts to the corrosive propellants, and that would start the clock on how long it could remain operable. So no, the individual APS engines were not fired before flight, but each component was tested, all possibly test were made that the assembly was correct, and unless a meteor hit the spacecraft in just the wrong spot—and probably even then—there was just no way that engine was not going to fire. And in spite of that, nails were chewed until it did.

Question: When Apollo 11 lifted off from the moon, was there any concern that the LM's ascent stage engine might not be powerful enough to get back into orbit, particularly with the extra weight of the lunar samples, and they might crash back onto the surface?
Answer: No. None at all. There was only concern at to whether it would fire and whether the computer would work, and since both had been tested to death, than concern was minimal. The power needed to lift off and return to orbit is simply math. And math isn’t trivial, but it had all been worked out by Konstantin Tsiolkovsky and published in 1903, so it wasn’t exactly new. Furthermore, and I’m a little surprised more people don’t know this, the Apollo astronauts weighed every sample they brought on board using a spring scale modified from a commercial scale used by anglers to weight their catch, and every piece of equipment returned to orbit or dumped on the lunar surface was accounted and planned for ahead of time. Mission planners knew with pretty good accuracy how much mass was returning to orbit, and that the margin of error was on the safe side.

Question: Why wasn't the Apollo 11 code written in higher programming languages like Fortran or COBOL?

It also needed an opperations staff. At MIT, an IBM 360/75 was used to emulate the AGC during development. That’s maybe not a completely fair comparison, but that computer weighed thousands of pound and consumed far more power than the entire Apollo CSM. Minicomputers were new. The PDP-8 didn’t have any full implementations of COBOL, but it could be programmed in FLOSS or FORTRAN. But a full system weighed 600 pounds (instead of 70) and consumed 500–1,000 watts (instead of 77). Don’t think of the ACG like a modern PC, or even a smart phone or an Arduino. Think of it like an embedded controller, or maybe a programmable calculator from the mid 1970s. It didn’t require all that much processing to get three highly-trained fighter pilots to the moon, and it certainly didn’t require a sophisticated user interface. The AGC did pretty simply things, Fire the engine at a certain power for a certain time, display a list of stars, rotate the spacecraft along this axis or that until its in such and such an orientation. All the hard calculation behind all that was done on the ground my a mainframe computer—in a high-level language like FORTRAN. That’s why all throughout the flight plan, there were “windows” and “gates”, moments when if the crew is to take an action like commit to land, commit to abort, or enter or leave orbit, that have to do it then; outside that window or paste the gate, the calculations haven’t been done and the AGC absolutely can not do them. Of course today, the CPU out of an XBOX could not on run the whole mission, but plan it on the fly.

Fungi appeared about a billion years ago, and seem to have specialized early as primarily decomposers, playing key roles in nutrient cycling in ecosystems. Plantae were hot on their heels, appearing around 1 billion to 700 million years ago, first as simple algea that took advantage of the colors of sunlight not used by other photosynthesyzers of the time. By 500 million years ago, simple plants had started to colonize the land. Animalia evolved between 700 and 600 million years ago, and soon (by 540 mya) their ability to concentrate nutrients and energy from other, simpler life forms led to an explosive growth in diversity and the appearance of all the basic body plans we see today (and many we don’t). Question: Though this may sound controversial and may be wrong, looking at humans like any other animal could there be different ‘species’ of humans still living? Like Black people in Africa, Asian people in Asia, white people in Europe and American Indian?
Answer: No, but also yes. “Species” is a completely arbitrary human categorization that had very little to do with actual life. It’s handy for teaching, managing and study, but it’s almost entirely arbitrary. In elementary school we often teach children that a species is a group of living things that can interbreed with each other. By that definition, all humans alive today and living for the last few tens of thousands of years all belong to the same species. Of course, that definition is wrong. Life doesn’t operates among distinct species, but among innumerable overlapping populations. All populations evolve by giving rise to variations, not all of which reproduce equally well in the particular circumstances in which they are living. When a population splits for any reason, whether some natural barrier, migration, or simply because some members are a little different and behave differently, the two new sub-populations start diverging as natural selection shapes them to fit the local environment. Neither the chicken nor the egg came first, both are part of the population of domestic chickens that slowly evolved from wild Southeast Asian red jungle fowl, eggs and all. But these sub populations are not by any reasonable definition new species, and they remain inter-fertile for a long time, sometimes tens or hundreds of thousands of years long. Many times, the populations will diverge, then run into each other and merge back together, enriching the master population. Other times, they continue to diverge, eventually becoming do distinct in biology, anatomy, and/or behavior, that they gradually become less and less inter-fertile. We humans usually divide them into distinct species long before the completely lose the ability to interbreed entirely, and in the fossil record, we can never know, so all of our species categories are just educated opinion. So, if whatever the professional union of taxanomic scientists were to get together and decide, say, red-headed step children from the Ilse of Wright are their own species, than they would be. This would not be an opinion supported by any evidence, though. Despite superficial differences like skin, eye, and hair color, we are all quite closely related, far closer than all the various varieties of domestic dog, say.

Question: Is the reason the Apollo 11 spacesuit force is so large (3 tons) compared to a 34 PSI on Earth for a bike tire because of the vacuum of space?
Answer: No, not at all. You just aren’t doing the math right. A kid’s bike may have tires inflated to 34 PSI because that’s all that’s needed to support the weight of the bike plus the kid. These tires are fairly fat, and if the kid and the bike together weight 68 pounds, the tires will flatten out just enough to make a combined 2 square inches of contact, providing exactly enough counter force to support that weight. If the little girl next door sits on the back, that might work too, though if the total weight is now 102 pounds, the tires will flatten out until a little less* than 3 square combined inches support that weight. But if dad climbs on, pushing the total weight to 204 pounds, the tires may not we able to flatten out enough to make a total of 6 square inches of contact without the rims touching the ground, and even if they can, that amount of deformation will cause a lot of extra wear and rolling resistance. That’s why dad rides a bike with tires inflated to 120 psi. If he and his bike weigh 150 pounds, the two tires will have a combined ground contact area of about 1.25 inches, exactly balancing that weight, and while the ride will be jarring unless over a very smooth surface, it’ll be fast. As an aside, your author rides a bike with tires meant to be inflated to 55 psi to support up to 300 lbs with a cushy, comfortable ride having 5.45 total square inches of ground contact. Good luck, anyone who tries that. I’, 6′ 1″, weigh 180 and inflate them to 65, for half that much ground contact and a much faster, though still rugged ride. I have no hope at all of keeping up with any racing or touring bike, but my last model survived 25,000 miles before the frame broke. But what’s that have to do with the Apollo 11 (A7L) spacesuit? Nothing. Except that pressure inflates spacesuits just like it does tires. The vacuum has absolutely nothing to do with it because tire pressures are relative to the atmosphere. So a tire inflated to 34 psi actually holds nearly 50, you just don’t feel the 14.7 or so being counterbalanced by the pressure of the air all around you. The air is pushing in on the tire by 14.7 psi, so that’s that much less force available to keep the tire from deforming when called upon to support weight. Spacesuits are used in vacuum, but that just means the pressure indicated it the real pressure, not just the effective (relative) pressure like in a tire here on Earth. When people talk about the force pushing out on the inside of a spacesuit being three tons, that’s pretty meaningless, because that’s the total pressure inflecting the total surface are of the suit. If you inflate a beach ball with a surface area of three square feet to 2 psi (relative to the atmosphere) the pressure pushing out is nearly 900 pounds; does that tell you anything? Does it stop you from squeezing it to use like a pillow? What counts in a beach ball is, is the pressure enough that it’ll bounce. What counts in a bike tire is, is the pressure enough to support the rider and bike without too much deformation. What counts in a spacesuit is, is the pressure enough to keep the astronaut alive, but not so much as to make the suit too stiff. If breathing pure oxygen, you only need about 4 psi to support life and activity, but there are a lot of square inches for that pressure to push against. Not all are equal, however. What really counts is, the pressure wants to inflate the suit in every direction, and you want to bend it into a normal body position for walking and going about your business. The force it takes to do that is not the total force pushing out on the suite, its the difference in the force pushing out in the suit in the fully inflated position versus the position you want it to be in. Let’s just say there really are three total tons ( call it 3,000 pounds) of force pushing out on the suit. When left to it’s own devices, it fully inflates, all limbs poking straight out, into the largest volume its structure permits. Now, if you are inside it and bend your elbow, you are reducing the inside volume by a little bit. If the volume change is 1%, you must apply 1% of the total force inflating the suit, or 1% or 3,000 lbs, or 30 lbs. So just bending your elbow is like curling a 30 lb dumbbell, you can do it, but man, it’s going to be tiring. So early spacesuits (like the A7L) used a system on straps and convolutes to minimize the change in volume as an astronaut moves. Think of a those silly inflatable man advertising gizmos compared to a wire reinforced air duct. Inflated to the same pressure, the duct will be much, much easier to bend because the wire hoops maintain its shape. Some newer spacesuits go one step further and use ‘constant volume joints.” These maintain the same volume no matter how they are bent by means of wedge shaped sections turning relative to one another on bearings. That are much more complex and imposed some limits on mobility, but completely eliminate the problem of having to struggle against the pressure every time you move. *A little less because squeezing the tire also increases the pressure slightly.

Question: What operating system did NASA use when man stepped on the moon and which one does he use now?
Answer: The Apollo Guidance Computers in the Command Module (the reentry capsule) and the LM (the lander) did not have an operating system. They booted and ran a bespoke program—actually, one of two: Luminary was responsible for the descent to the lunar surface, lunar surface operations, and ascent back to the Command Module in lunar orbit. Colossus handled main spacecraft operations including navigation, guidance, and control during most of the mission phases such as trans-lunar injection, lunar orbit insertion, and the return to Earth. It provided support for the primary mission phases except those specific to the lunar landing and ascent. Ad operating system is a program (or usually, a system of programs) running (usually) atop a hardware interface layer (such as the BIOS of the IBM PC) that acts as a platform in which independent, often cross-platform) applications can be installed and run without having to bother with all the technical minutia of the hardware they are on. The IBM 360 mainframe on the ground ran OS 360, an operating system of exactly this sort that not only provided a support environment for applications, it provided isolated virtual address spaces for time-sharing users, who in turn got to run programs and applications almost as if on their own machine. Decades later, I worked on COBOL programs running on a great grandchild of the same operating system that believed they were talking to us through punched cards and paper tape. That’s because those were the only input/output methods when the system was first created, and all those years later, the operating system maintained the illusion to keep the old applications happy. But operating systems introduce a HUGE amount of overhead. Part of this is because they tend to bloat, and part of it’s because they have to do a LOT of work to buffer the applications from the hardware. My little chromebook running Mint is way more efficient than your Windows box because Mint is a variant of Linnux designed to be efficient—it doesn’t do any of the unnecessary crap Windows does like spying on you and guessing what music you want to hear, it just does what the hell I tell it when the hell I tell it. But my Apply IIe was way more efficient still, because it’s operating system (and architecture) were so much simpler and in particular, because most applications ran the video memory in text mode instead of graphics mode like most operating systems today, so instead of a few hundred numbers per character, they had one—its ASCII code. But the computer I designed and built for my high school science fair robot was way, way, way more efficient than that. It didn’t have any operating system at all. As soon as power was applied, it executed a bootstrap rourine and went into a loop, checking for input from the keyboard and ready to follow hardward interrupts triggered by the cassette interface or any of the robot’s sensors. And that’s exactly how the AGC worked. It didn’t need an operating system, because all the software that would ever be run on it was written by the same people who were building the hardware, so the two evolved together and were designed intricately for each other. This made for super efficient code execution, if rather cumbersome maintenance. Software was woven into rope memory, mounted in a module, tested, an potted in plastic to survive the rigors of space. If you later found a bug, needed to make and update, or just wanted to run the other program, you had to crack open the case and swap the memory module. And you could only use one compatible with the hardware version of your AGC, so rapid application development it wasn’t.

Question: Even at 4.3 PSI, would the space suit be rigid and immobilize the astronauts?
Answer: Let’s look at a related, but simpler question. When the Apollo astronauts were suited up and ready to go out on the surface, they opened the valve to vent the cabin, unlatched the door and pulled—and the door wouldn’t open. Why? Because with a valve open to hard vaccume, but the evaporators in their suits emitting a trickle of water vapor, the pressure inside was too high until they were able to pry up a corner of the door and break the seal. Then the cabin vented all of a sudden, letting the door fly open. The hatch was 32 inches wide, or 1,024 square inches (0.65 sq. meters). The pressure inside bottomed out at about 0.1 psi, but that’s still 102 pounds of force holding the hatch closed. On later missions, they opened the valves on both the hatches and had a slightly easier time. So, with this illustrative example in mind, let’s consider your much more complicated question. The surface area of an adult human arm is somewhere in the neighborhood of 125 square inches (800 square cm). At 4.3 PSI, that’s 537 pounds pushing outward around the arm. Not all of that force resists bending the joints, however; to estimate that force, assume the arm can be approximated as a cylinder and that the bending force acts over the cross-sectional area of the cylinder. Then you get 54 pounds. So to move the shoulder joint or elbow joint to any position other than straight out takes about the force of lifting a full bucket of river rock on Earth, or close to three buckets to simultaneously flex the shoulder, elbow and wrist, assuming the spacesuit lacks constant volume joints and other movement aids. You can do that in the pinch, maybe once, and then you’re pretty much done for unless your a recent Mr. Universe contestant.

Question: Assuming air resistance to be negligible, if two objects A and B (B has more mass) are dropped from the same height on earth wouldn't B reach the ground faster since it's kinetic energy (on impact) would be higher than A?
Answer: No, and that’s tells us something. Say you have object B which has twice the mass of object A and you plan to drop both in a vacuum chamber. Object B is heavier than A, which is another way of saying it takes twice as much force to hold it before the drop; it takes twice as much force to stop it from falling. This means that when released, twice as much force will accelerate it toward the ground, right? However, twice as much mass means twice as much inertia. Inertia is the property of matter that keeps it moving (or not moving) at the same speed in the same direction unless acted on. It take twice as much force to accelerate something with twice as much inertia by the same amount. So when dropped, object B will be accelerated by twice as much gravitational attraction but will resist that acceleration by twice as much inertia. It will therefore accelerate at precisely the same rate as object A, or for that matter, a grain of dust or a feather dropped beside it. Why precisely that same? Why does gravitational attraction vary with mass by exactly—exactly—the same amount as inertia? Well, this is the conventional, Newtonian conception of gravity. if Einstein was right¹, the answer is that the attraction and the inertia are the same because they are literally the same thing. You see, in Einstein’s theory, there is no such thing as a force of gravity. Rather, we live in a universe in which time and space are just dimensions of a common whole. We are all moving together through spacetime. An isolated and stationary object would only be stationary in space—its inertia would carry it forward in a straight line through time at a constant speed. But mass warps spacetime. A stationary object near a massive planet is not pulled toward the planet by gravity, rather, its inertia continues to carry it forward through spacetime, but since space is now curved “outward” away from the planet, a straight path forward through spacetime is a path curving down through space toward the planet. That change in direction of motion and is resisted by the object’s inertia is exactly the same way the inertia of a bicycle resists the change when entering the curve in a velodrome, and so feels like a centrifugal force pushing the bike out against the floor. In a little more detail, if our object A, object B, dust mote and feather all are near Earth, all continue moving in a straight line at the same speed through time. But since spacetime near the planet is curved, they all follow the same curved path through spacetime, and unless something stops them, we see that as acceleration toward the planet. They all experience the same acceleration not because of a common external force (gravity), but because their paths through spacetime are all curving at the same rate. As long as we don’t get in the way, they all act exactly the same², whether moving out in near-Earth space or together inside a vacuum chamber on the ground. You mentioned the kinetic impact when they hit the ground. This too is really just inertia in action. An object sitting on the ground is being deflected through spacetime by the ground. It experiences a constant change in direction (through spacetime) because the ground prevents it following the straight path through spacetime we would see as “falling.” So there is no actual force holding it down, rather, its own inertia is resisting downward motion through space (linear, forward motion through spacetime) in direct proportion to its mass (because inertia is a property of mass). So what about when a falling object hits the ground? Well, just as gravity looks to us like an attractive force, even through it’s really just inertia in spacetime, kinetic energy looks like a form of “potential energy” even through it too is really just inertia. When permitted to fall (especially through a vacuum), an object follows a straight path through spacetime, but because that spacetime is warped by the planet, it appears to an observer as acceleration toward the planet. The longer is accelerates, the greater the difference in velocity through ordinary space between object and planet. So when the object hits the ground, the ground will no only halt its continued acceleration but equalize the velocity and direction of the object with the ground—both of which are resisted by the inertia of the object. Kinetic energy isn’t an actual form of energy, it’s just an imbalance in velocity that, when equalized, will take energy to overcome inertia. Now, from everything I have read, Einstein indeed believed this was literally true, and it’s supported by all the evidence available to us to extraordinarily great precision. It still might not be true, and it certainly isn’t the whole story. But it’s important, because if true in any sense, then there is no gravitational force in the sense of the other forced of nature, there is no such thing as a graviton, and gravity cannot (probably) be quantized, which means were still have a lot of physics to work out.

Question: Does a bathroom easily become mouldy even with a window open? Should water be completely removed quickly after someone takes a shower in one?
Answer: Unless you live in the tropics, no part of your home interior should mold—really ever unless you have a leave to do something unwise like hang wet towels where they can touch the wall. And if you live where it’s arid, you may not need any ventilation to stop mold growing from normal bathing use—the water will all go into solution in the dry air. So how much ventilation you need depends on how much moisture you put in the and and how much moisture that air can absorb. But no, under no circumstances should the bathroom become moldy from normal use, and if its growing enough mold for you to see and clean, it might be growing molds elsewhere that you can’t see, or even be providing moisture to insects. However, at least in the United States, while building codes have gotten slightly stricter over the years (bathroom vents are no longer allowed to vent into the attic, which can cause mold growth, ice damage, and insulation damage) but they still do not take climate into account. Down in the south where humidity is usually high, the codes don’t require anywhere near enough ventilation to prevent mold in a bathroom containing a shower. Newer homes are required to have powered vents, but the volume of air they can move is really designed to control toilet odor, not mold, and there is no requirement that fans be run long enough to do their job. Most such fans are integrated with lights, and are while cheap but noisy—with a build-in incentive to keep the fan too small. Worse, newer homes are tight to reduce air infiltration and reduce heating and cooling costs. That’s fine, but it reduces the effectiveness of exhaust fans because it’s harder for replacement air to enter the house. So…while this is something contractors and the industry are now paying more attention to, most Southern homes, even upscale homes, have crappy bathroom ventilation. I’ve dealt with this problem in homes in Louisiana and Texas, where mold and mildew are guaranteed in any room with a shower that isn’t properly ventilated. When I bought my current home, built in 1994 in a nice upscale suburb, it had no vent at all over the master shower, only the code-required vent over the toilet, located behind a door and on the other side of the rather large bathroom. Every time we used the shower, warm, moist air would rise toward the high ceilings and condense out on the walls, forming visible streaks and growing mold. I cleaned and disinfected, then I Googled the “correct” size for ventilation of a bathroom of the size and installed an in-line vent in the attic — whisper quiet and controlled by a timer to it would run for a few minutes after ever showed to help exhaust the moisture. It helped, but not enough to stop the drips and annual cleaning with bleach. A few years passed and we were getting ready to renovate the master bath. At the same time, my kids had become teens and started showering, and even their much smaller bathroom was growing mold like crazy with the cheap, noisy fan/light installed by the builder. So I bought a new fan for the master, one with twice the generally recommended capacity. I had to cut a second intake so we have one over the shower and one beside it, both joined by a union in the ductwork. Then I took the old fan—half the capacity but still several times that of the cheaper contractor fan, and installed it in the girl’s bathroom. Now I had a new problem. Any time either fan operated, I could smell musty dust being sucked down around the attic access door. So I added weatherstripping to that door, and I installed a baffled passive duct to allow replacement air to enter the house but without letting vermin in (and with a magnetic flap that closes when not in use to prevent passive movement of air). And now, two years later, the problem is finally solved. We have no condensation in either bathroom, no mold, and no attic smell. I’m handy, and it took several small projects and a fair amount of research to get it the way the contractor should have done it to begin with.

Name: C Stuart Hardwick
Question: Is there something beyond gamma rays?
Answer: Hell yeah. Gamma rays represent the highest energy portion of the electromagnetic spectrum that is typically studied in the context of traditional electromagnetic bands, so no distinct "band" above gamma rays, is generally recognized. However. . . Gamma rays have frequencies over 10^19 hertz (Hz), with wavelengths shorter than 10 picometers (trillionths of meters) and extending into the exahertz (quintillionths of a meter) range, but it’s not terribly meaningful to talk about wavelengths when they get that short. Instead, gamma ray photons and above are generally describes by the energy of a single photon. For comparison, a photon of green light has an energy of about 2.5 electron volts. Phenomena such as gamma ray bursts and other energetic astrophysical events can produce radiation with energies in the trillion electron volt range. Some authors call these “cosmic rays” but that’s ambiguous as the term is also used to describe other types of high energy interstellar radiation consisting of charged particles, such as protons and atomic nuclei (mostly hydrogen nuclei) traveling at near light speed. On the other hand, on October 15, 1991, the Fly's Eye Experiment, a cosmic ray observatory in Utah, USA, detected an ultra-high-energy cosmic ray with an estimated energy of approximately 3.2×10^20 electron volts, or 320 exa-electron volts. This is orders of magnitude higher than anything achievable in particle accelerators on Earth, and is comparable to the most energetic photons released by cosmic events. Indeed, it’s close to the theoretical upper limit (the Greisen-Zatsepin-Kuzmin cutoff), which is the maximum energy that cosmic rays can attain due to interactions with cosmic microwave background radiation during their propagation through space. There is no theoretical upper limit to the energy that a single photon can have—except (thanks Mike for reminding me) it presumably can’t have have a wavelength shorter than the Planck length, which corresponds to an energy of 10^19 billion electron volts, which is….a lot.

Question: What are the differences between visible light and gamma rays?
Answer: The difference between visible light (the range of electromagnetic radiation we can see) and gamma rays (the range emitted by powerful nuclear and cosmic events) is: This means that gamma rays are quite useful, but unit for unit, are almost indescribably more dangerous to living things than optical light. Optical photons can’t break chemical bonds directly, unlike gamma rays and all frequencies above visible light*, so they can’t directly damage genes or injure living cells. Instead can only deliver heat when absorbed. *Even light at the bottom of the UV band (between visible light and x-rays) can only alter chemical bonds under special circumstances like when a single atom happens to absorb two photons at the same time. That’s why UV-A helps you tan and make vitamine D, but can damage your skin with too much exposure, while UV-B light can cause sunburn and cancer and UV-C light can destroy living cells outright just like x-rays and gamma rays, but unlike visible light. That’s why we often call infrared light “radiant heat” and cook our dinners with microwaves. UV-B photons (which can only barely affect chemical bonds) have five times the energy of infrared photons, so infrared can’t hurt you unless you get too close to something hot and get burned. Hot things emit in the infrared, and you are neither reflective nor transparent to it, to it does a good job of heating you up. Food is mostly transparent to microwave energy, so by bouncing it around and around inside a metal box, you can heat your food from the inside. This is handy, but it absolutely will not give you cancer, and these photons contain only 1/10,000th as much energy as UV-B. Now, you could try to build a gamma ray oven, but I wouldn’t recommend it. Gamma rays will pass through matter just like microwaves, and while it’s much, much harder to do, it might be possible to build a container they would bounce around in enough times to eventually be largely absorbed by say a pot roast. This would be a very, very bad idea. Where microwaves will heat the roast from inside, infrared light will heat it from the outside, and optical light will make it pretty on the table, a gamma ray oven might heat it, but would also break it down chemically into a radioactive chemical gruel bearing little culinary similarity to meat.

Question: What is the most primitive human that a modern day human couldn't successfully procreate with?
Answer: What constitutes "human" varies by the context and the criteria being used. In a biological sense, Homo sapiens is the only surviving species of the genus Homo that is commonly referred to as "human" in everyday language. Neanderthals (Homo neanderthalensis) and other members of the Homo genus, such as Homo erectus and Homo habilis, are considered close relatives or ancestors of modern humans but are not classified as Homo sapiens. Very roughly, “the most primitive human that a modern day human couldn’t successfully procreate with” would be anyone who says “no” and is armed or strong enough to keep you off them. However, it's worth noting that Neanderthals and other ancient hominins displayed complex behaviors, tool use, social structures, and even cultural practices that indicate a level of sophistication and intelligence akin to modern humans. Therefore, in a broader sense, some researchers might consider them as part of the broader human family tree. The term "human" can thus be used in a more inclusive way to encompass all members of the genus Homo. By this measure then, and very roughly, “the most primitive human that a modern day human couldn’t successfully procreate would be from the population of apes we call Homo habilis, which lived approximately 2.1 to 1.5 million years ago in Eastern Africa, primarily in present-day Kenya, Ethiopia, and Tanzania. It’s not absolutely certain that successful interbreeding would be absolutely impossible, it’s very unlikely on both genetic, anatomical, and behavioral grounds. That said, I highly suspect that what you meant to ask is, “what’s the most primitive human that a modern day human could successfully procreate with?” And the answer might still be Homo habilis, because as I say, it might not be impossible, perhaps if you traveled back with a time machine and a collection of alcohol and Barry White records intent on reinvigorating the modern human genome. I suspect however, there might be easier ways to go about it. One would certainly be to take your time machine to visit the Neanderthals with a bag of beef jerky on offer. We know from direct genetic evidence we did interbreed with them, though not very much. This argues against Homo erectus (1.9 mya to 143,000 years ago), but Homo heidelbergensis (600,000 to 200,000 years ago) and Homo antecessor (1.2 mya …) might be better candidate, as both appear more closely related to the population that gave rise to us, as opposed to that which branched off to give Neanderthalensis.

Name: C Stuart Hardwick
Question: Having a new species require at least 2 mutated species (male and female) with same characteristics, and they need to be around the same area to have any chance of mating. If it is that difficult, how are there so many species on earth today?
Answer: Congratulations. You have just demonstrated you understand fuck all about evolution. Species is a human construct, invented to simplify talking about something complex. We teach elementary school children that a species is a group of living things that can’t breed with any other, and while that’s often true, we too often neglect telling the children that it’s an oversimplification and returning to the topic later to explain more fully, and so years later our children grow up to ask questions like this one. No. Your understanding of species is wrong. Forget about species. Evolution is the result of living populations reproducing with variation and not all variants surviving equally well. Over time, populations can split for any number of reasons, from trekking off to find green pastures to stumbling over a waterfall to getting chased out of the valley by lava. However it happens, the two subpopulations keep evolving, now to become better suited to two different environments. Given enough time, they will inevitably become so different they can no longer interbreed with each other if given the chance. Long before that happens, they will generally lose interest in doing so, and anyway, they generally can’t try because of whatever split them apart. But if they can, they often do, and populations once split later meet up and blend back together all the time. Whether two populations are different enough to be called distinct species by humans is not something nature knows or cares about. Nature is just living populations, changing, evolving, splitting, combining, slowly growing to conform to their local environment. Species do not, as you imagine, pop into being through a single event, but emerge slowly through gradual changes to the population. At some point, humans come along and decide where to draw the lines, or find fossils and guess, but that’s not what matters. What matters is the living populations, and the change.

Name: C Stuart Hardwick
Question: If evolution is spurred by natural selection, a selection is a choice, and to make a choice you have to be a conscious thinking being. What, or who, is making that selection? If it is nature, wouldn't nature have to be a conscious living entity?
Answer: Question: If evolution is spurred by natural selection… Answer: Yes… Assertion: a selection is a choice— Reality: No. Stop right there. If there’s an earthquake and you die without having children because the ground opens up and swallows you, that’s not a choice; you were standing in the wrong place at the wrong time, woe is you, but you are still selected out of the gene pool, goodbye, thanks for playing. Natural selection is the filter of survival. It makes no more conscious choice than a crack in a swimming pool “chooses” which water molecules leak out. Some do, some don’t. It depends on how near they are and what they are stuck to or mixed with. Evolution is the amplification of the traits of survivors. Sometimes they survive to get amplified by having some trait that makes them a tiny bit better at not getting dead than their neighbors, say by being a little more squeamish about going about when the ground is all rumbly. But many times, much of the time in fact, the survivors are just standing in the right spot watching some other poor sot fall down a crevasse when the Earth gets all in a tizzy. Assertion: to make a choice you have to be a conscious thinking being. Reality: Really? So the sun consciously decided to rise in the east? The Mississippi consciously decided to abandon the thirty some odd channels it’s taken in the distant past? The steel balls in pinball and pachinko machines consciously decide whether to give you points? A uranium atom consciously decides when to decay? No, dear reader, shit happens, and sometimes when it happens to you, your luck runs out permanent like. Question: If it is nature, wouldn't nature have to be a conscious living entity? Answer: No. Sorry. The world doesn’t work that way, and playing semantic games wouldn’t change the way the world works even if you had the semantics correct, which you don’t. All living populations reproduce with variation. Those variations go out into the world and face threats and scarce resources and do well or not so well, consciously, unconsciously, or even as stupidly as the most ignorant evolution denier. Those that do well pass on their traits more successfully than those who don’t, and small changes add up to big changes. Believe it or don’t, nature isn’t conscious and wouldn’t care anyway whether you wake up and accept the world you live in or not. Only being smart enough to study and understand reality is our strength, we humans, and if you refuse to do that because reality rubs you the wrong way, really may very well rub you and yours out, and small loss to the rest of us that may be.
