Question: Why do people think Europe is a continent?
Answer: People think Europe is a continent because since ancient times, Europe has been considered a continent. A continent is one of several large landmasses, traditionally as separated by geographical features such as oceans or mountain ranges, but today increasingly defined by the boundaries of continental tectonic plates. These plates are fragments of crust floating atop the slowly roiling mantle, and often pushed along by the continually moving and recycling basalt of the ocean floor. Tectonic plates give a natural measure of geographic fragmentation, but is doesn’t always reflect cultural and trade divisions of historic importance to people, and so isn’t the final determinant. The seven traditionally recognized continents on Earth are: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, and Australia. India is generally considered to be part of Asia, but is often called a subcontinent and sits on its own tectonic plate. There is some debate as to whether Zealandia, including New Zealand and New Caldonia, should be considered a distinct continent as well. In the case of Europe, it and most of Asia sit on the same tectonic plate, but we’ve only known that for forty years, and the concept of continents has been around for millennia. The ancient Greeks for example, recognized the continents of Europe, Asia, and Africa, but only from fragmentary reports. They didn't know that Europe and Asia were connected, and had no idea that plate tectonics was a thing. Even though on the same continental plate, Europe and Asia are separated by the Ural mountains and by vast stretches of steppe that were not very accommodating or valuable to the great trading nations of the age of discovery, and so were a formidable social and geologic barrier. It wasn't until the age of exploration and cartography that the exact nature of continental boundaries and connections became clearer. By the time it was known that Europe and Asia were part of the same landmass, they had already been enshrined by cart ographers as distinct for thousands of years. Today, geologists sometimes refer to Eurasia, while sociologists etc. still treat Europe and Asia as distinct. In the end, words mean what it is useful for them to mean, and what is useful can vary by context.

Question: How did they photograph Neal Armstrong setting foot on the moon?

When he reached the porch, he pulled a cord which released a latch which let the shelf fall open—simple. Mounted this way, the camera was upside down, and controllers had to flip a switch to electronically invert the image. TV cameras were far too heavy and power hungry to fit the requirements of the mission, so the camera was custom engineered to fit strict limits on size, weight, power consumption, and bandwidth. It did this by using miniaturization techniques that had not yet reached the commercial market and a number of design simplifications like the substitution of robust, high fidelity components normally used in TV camera with smaller semiconductors that could so the same job, just not as well or for as long. In addition, the resolution and frame rate were reduced to fit the broadcast within a narrow slice of the S-band transmission back to Earth. No technology existed for converting this non-standard analog format to the standard NTSC signal used at the time, so once received by the large dish antennas of the Deep Space Network, the image was displayed on a super-bright screen and re-captured using a standard TV camera for broadcast to the networks.

Question: Modern commercial airplanes artificial horizon is corrected for Earth Curvature. Would small propeller airplane like Cessna artificial horizon drift due to Earth rotation over longer time?

So starting in the 1930, artificial horizons were based on a gyro that would maintain a fixed orientation no matter what the aircraft did around it. These were much better, but has to be adjusted for procession over time and importantly, the change in current “down” direction while flying long distances around the Earth. The latter is accomplished by having small weights (pendulous vanes) that apply a small, steady pressure to steer the gyro to stay true to the current direction of gravity. In the short run, a plane can roll and pitch and do acrobatics and the gyro will hold the artificial horizon steady. Question: Can evolution produce new genes? If the answer is yes, what are the examples and evidence?
Answer: Yes, evolution can produce new genes. Here is a case in point that we happened to stumble across recently. A common soil bacteria was found living in a chemical holding pond near a chemical plant. Th bacterium was of a species that lives all over the world, but it was weird finding it in the pond where there we essentially no nutrients to sustain it. It turns out, two mutations explained it. First, a replication error had duplicated a gene for an enzyme needed for metabolizing nutrients in the muddy water filling roadside ditches where the bacteria normally live. This didn’t hurt anything, it just gave the bacteria an unneeded extra supply of this vital enzyme and wastes a little of its energy. Later, a frame shift mutation (another mistake in copying, probably caused by chemical instability lingering from the first mutation) changed the meaning of the gene, causing it to create a new garbled enzyme that was useless out in the ditch—but since it was surplus, that didn’t make any difference either. However, it just so happened that the garbles enzyme was able to fit to a chemical byproduct of the manufacture of Nylon, a chemical that had never existed on Earth until the 20th century, but that existed in abundance in the holding pond. The garbles enzyme didn’t fit this molecule very well, but it fit well enough to let the microbe feed on it very inefficiently. That didn’t matter though, because there was a whole ocean of it right next door that none of the other bacteria could use—a whole new uncontested biological niche, just waiting to be exploited. Neither of these mutations were rare. Genes duplications and frame shift mutations happen all the time in every living population. When useless, they eventually get swept away by natural pruning processes. When useful, they become amplified by reproductive success, as when a mutant bacteria is able to colonize a vacant niche as in this example, where selective pressure will inevitably lead to a more efficient enzyme through additional mutations, provided the pond remains there long enough. Indeed, this exact sort of thing is why we have deposits of coal today. About 360 million years ago, some series of mutations created the polymer lignin in plants, and woody plants appeared. Nothing on Earth could break down this novel polymer, so when plants died, they just sat there until they were buried and fossilized, burned, or baked into charcoal as heavy living overburden burned atop them. This went on for 60 million years until mutations in some bacteria and fungi let them break down lignin and feed on the remains of woody plants, which they do to this very day.

Question: Why didn't the Hiroshima and Nagasaki nuclear bombs leave any deep craters? Shouldn't they have?

Detonation at the surface generates outward force in all directions, of which upward and outward offer the least resistance by far. The trinity test shot, fired from a steel tower only 100 feet high only dug a crater about 10 feet deep even though it was fired over the loose sand of the Jornada del Muerto desert. When surface explosions create a crater, it’s either because they are somehow designed to direct force into the surface (as in a shaped explosive charge) or the surface is comparatively soft. For example, the Beirut explosion of a warehouse full of fertilizer excavated a crater 140 meters (460 feet) in diameter and approximately 43 meters (141 feet) deep, and was only a bit less powerful the the to atomic bombings. But the building sat on the water, on reclaimed land of mostly water logged sand and the force of the blast was initially constrained by the shear mass of 2,750 tons of ammonium nitrate, 23 tons of fireworks, 5 rolls of detonation cord, and 1,000 vehicle tires, all acting as a tamper to slow the expansion of the shockwave early in the event. The Port Chicago disaster of 1944 was caused by the explosion of approximately 4,600 tons of munitions, including bombs and ammunition and released an energy comparable to 5 kilotons of TNT. It destroyed the pier, nearby ships, and surrounding structures, but did not create a visible crater because the force was directed outward and upward, resulting in widespread destruction of the port facilities and nearby infrastructure.

Question: Why does the shorter wavelength scatter more in the atmosphere than the long wavelength? Is it related to intensity?
Answer: No, nor is it even any spooky quantum mechanics. It’s actually a straightforward interaction between light (which has an electric field component) and the electrons in the molecules of air, (which have charge). The electric field of the light wave influences charges (electrons) within the atmosphere to oscillate at the same frequency as the incoming light wave. If the electrons are able to move under this stimulation (if the molecules are much smaller than the wavelength of the light) the moving electric field generates a new electromagnetic ripple at the same frequency—or put another way, photons of light of the same color are emitted, but in a random direction. Thus, the higher the frequency of light, the more it is scattered by molecules of nitrogen and oxygen, so the sky appears blue, the sun (robbed of a bit of blue by this scattering) appears yellow, and sunsets (denuded of blue by a lot of scattering over a long distance) appear red. But clouds and overcast skies appear white or gray because they contain tiny water droplets (or ice crystals) which scatter yellow and red wavelengths along with the nitrogen and oxygen molecules scattering bluer colors, so all the colors are scattered about equally.

Question: Does the Space Force train in space?

That said, as an Air Force Command and Staff College instructor told me in 2018, just before creation of the Space Force, wherever people go, the law and the military will soon follow. This was, honestly, overly conservative. Many people don’t realize that the Space Force was not dreamed up by Donald Trump and it was not created lightly. It actually resulted from bipartisan efforts stretching back to the 1980s, and indeed, Air Force Space Command was created at that time. The role of the Space Force is to safeguard access to space and assets in space for the benefit of the United States and its allies. That doesn’t just mean military space, but all the billions of dollars worth of satellites that are now indispensable to the economy and modern life, from getting pizza delivered to keeping the clocks current in ATMs and all sorts of remote computer terminals, helping keep communications secure. Far too many Americans seem to think the answer to war it to just stop giving money to the military. It isn’t. The undeniable lessons of two world wars are that the way to prevent war is by maintaining the ability to win, should anyone dare to start it, and never getting yourself into a position where you are tempted to appease belligerents—who will then be emboldened. Too many focus on cost overruns and policy mistakes and mis the fact that the United States maintains a military that, while obviously large and expensive, is on the whole extremely well-managed, reliable, and professional. It isn’t always used wisely, but it’s effective, and much of the cost is the price we pay for only needing 2–3% of the population serving at any given time, at least in peacetime. Critical to this underappreciated peace dividend are our constellations of reconnaissance, communications, and positioning satellites, which together let us ward off surprise aggression, rapidly response when we must, and delivery violence directly onto the heads of bad actors instead of only cities using area bombardment or weapons of mass destruction. Most American’s just don’t get how important this is to our livelihoods and peace, but Russia and China sure do. Both have tested satellite systems designed to destroy, jamb, or tamper with our satellites, and several other nations have tested anti-satellite weapons as well. The Space Force was created because experts in Congress became convinced that the Air Force just wasn’t putting enough emphasis on space defense, and now its working to correct that. Far from worrying that it’s all some boondoggle to put unneeded “boots in orbit” (it isn’t) Americans and citizens of allied nations ought more properly to be concerned that the Space Force is now playing catch up—and hope that doesn’t bite us all in the ass. The Space Force won’t have much use for soldiers in space any time soon, but it absolutely SHOULD be developing a rapid interdiction system using storable (solid rocket) launch vehicles capable of orbiting robotic or even crewed threat responses fast—like on a few hours notice—because sooner or later, we will need it. For more on the mission and convoluted origins on the Space Force, including the real sources of its iconography and uniform, check out Tales of the United States Space Force, coming in June 2024 from Baen Books and Simon & Schuster, with great science fiction illustrating why we need a Space Force, and articles busting myths about it.

Question: Why are people freaking about the solar eclipse?
Answer: Are people freaking? There won’t be another total solar eclipse visible from North America until Aug. 23, 2044, and it won’t be as good, as the moon won’t be as close to Earth and the path of totality will only cross three states. Certainly, it won’t be an easy drive from my house, if I’m still around. Why’s it a big deal? Well for a start, total eclipses that are observable from land are rare enough to still of genuine scientific interest. For most people, it’s just something to go see and do together, with or without a well-informed understanding. For those of us who have that understanding, it is if nothing else, a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to see nature in palpable motion. Here are my observations from the eclipse of April 8, 2024: My wife and I were at a cabin in Bend, Texas, far from the crowds and almost exactly in the center of the path of totality. In preceding days, we'd explored central Texas from Fredericksburg to San Saba, watching the weather and cloud cover forecasts like hawks, debating where we might drive to at the last minute if the outlook didn't improve. Finally, with cloud cover forecast at around 50-70% throughout the region, we elected to stay put in a little zip-code-sized window of clarity that had arisen in forecasts based on CONUS satellite data northwest of Austin, and Mother Nature didn't disappoint. From first contact to totality, the skies were almost totally clear, and we had great viewing of the advancing eclipse through safety glasses, a pinhole camera, and even natural projections beneath the trees (see below). But that wasn't what we'd come for. Five minutes before second contact--before the moment commencing totality--we walked down the hundred or so feet to the dry rock bed lining the eponymous bend in the Colorado River. Already, it was noticeably dark, chill, and quiet as clouds rolled beneath the darkening sky in passing clumps. Then, like sunset running in super fast-forward, the butterflies vanished, the songbirds fell silent, and the western sky went salmon, then grey. A lone vulture fell from his flagging thermal and flapped northward along the river, then the largest grouping of vultures I've ever seen--probably fifty birds--clustered in a last thermal behind us to the east, but it was clear they were struggling to maintain altitude and soon they sought roosts as darkness fell. Now, with the sun's shadow growing to the northwest and waning to the southeast, the wind, which had consistently gusted from the east toward the warm updrafts over the open bed of the Colorado, shifted to out of the west as the frogs and the crickets along the cooling river sang nighttime music. Up at the cabin, the automatic hanging yard lights had come on, and it really looked like night, darker than Houston an hour after sunset when the horizon is just fading and the city lights become visible against the clouds. There were no city lights anywhere near here. But all to soon, the western sky grew light, roosters crowed north of us, and in a few seconds it was dawn, then morning. The clicking calls of the cricket frog fell silent and an early Bewick's Wren returned to his song along the river. Soon, birdsong again filled the river basin and vultures the skies, and a pair of fat lizards chased each other happily across the black, sun-warmed rocks. And we were packing for home. Totality lasted a whopping 4 minutes, 13 seconds, a momentary night that I will never, ever forget.

Question: Technically speaking, during a total eclipse, is the moon covering 100% of the sun? Or is it more? Or is it less?
Answer: During a total eclipse, from the perspective of people looking from within the path of totality, the moon appears to cover more than 100% of the surface of the sun. The moon doesn’t orbit Earth in the same plane we orbit the sun, so we only experience an eclipse when the two planes happen to intersect while the moon is new (between Earth and the sun). When the alignment is poor, we get a partial eclipse, but when the alignment is just right, the moon and sun line up perfectly for a short time and we see a total eclipse. But not all total eclipses are the same. The moon is far smaller than the sun but is much closer, and its distance from Earth varies by thousands of miles as it moves through its not-quite-circular orbit around Earth. When its at its farthest, its too far away to fully block the sun and we see an annular eclipse—a ring of the outer sun shining around the moon. When the moon is at its nearest, it completely blocks the sun and even part of its outer atmosphere, but only from the perspective of those on Earth who are right “beneath” it, and so are sheltered from enough sunlight that the scattering of light in Earth’s atmosphere cannot turn the whole sky blue.

Question: Atheists always say they are backed by science, but can their science explain why it rains?
Answer: Imagine the sky as a giant sponge. This sponge can hold a lot of water vapor, which is like invisible water floating around in the air. When this sponge gets really full, it starts to wring itself out, just like when you squeeze a wet sponge. That's when it rains! Now, here's how it works: the sun heats up the Earth, especially water like lakes, rivers, and oceans. This heat makes the water turn into vapor—a gas—which rises up into the sky. As the vapor goes higher, it cools down and turns back into tiny water droplets. These droplets form clouds. This keeps happening until eventually, the droplets start bumping together and growing until they are too heavy to stay aloft and fall as rain. Ice crystals, dust, or soot (say, from a passing airplane) can seed cloud formation and accelerate the development of rain. Changes in temperature and pressure can vary the amount of water vapor the air can hold and so also influence the formation of clouds and rain. So, again in simple terms, rain happens when the air gets too full of water and the clouds can't hold it anymore, so they let it all out as raindrops. Rain that doesn’t evaporate runs off into lakes and rivers, trickles into underground reserviors, and eventually reaches the ocean. But sooner or later, water near the surface evaporates again and heads back up to the clouds. This is called the hydrologic cycle and is critical to life. An that’s just a little—highly simplified—of what science tells us about why it rains. Science, by the way, is just checking reality to see what’s true.
